why.correct: The masses differ by about 2 g/mol and the electron counts by at most 2, but the boiling points span 98 °C. Something other than mass or dispersion forces must differ: the kinds of attraction.
options: Right: nearly equal masses with very different boiling points rule out mass as the explanation.
This is the "molar mass alone" error. 1-Propanol is only 2 g/mol heavier than butane, far too little to explain a 98 °C difference.
Acetone has the fewest electrons but boils in the middle, above butane, so electron count does not set the order here.
The data show no such trend, and the masses are too close for mass to set the order in either direction.

why.correct: Acetone's C=O bond makes the molecule polar, so its molecules also attract by dipole-dipole forces. Butane is nonpolar. With similar electron counts, the extra dipole-dipole attraction explains the higher boiling point.
options: Right: the extra kind of attraction is dipole-dipole.
Acetone has an O atom but no H bonded to O, N or F, so its molecules cannot hydrogen-bond to each other.
Acetone has 32 electrons, two fewer than butane, so dispersion forces cannot explain its higher boiling point.
Boiling separates whole molecules; no covalent bond, C=O or C–C, breaks when a liquid boils.

why.correct: 1-Propanol has electrons (dispersion), is polar (dipole-dipole), and has H bonded to O with lone pairs on O (hydrogen bonds). It has no ions.
options: Right: dispersion forces act between all particles.
Right: 1-propanol is a polar molecule because of its C–O–H group.
Right: the H on O of one molecule is attracted to a lone pair on the O of another.
Ion-dipole forces need an ion, and pure 1-propanol is made of neutral molecules.
Covalent bonds hold atoms together inside a molecule; separate molecules attract, they do not share electrons.

why.correct: Boiling overcomes intermolecular forces. The O–H bond matters because it lets the molecule form hydrogen bonds with its neighbors, but it does not break.
options: Right: covalent bonds do not break when a liquid boils.
O–H bonds are in fact strong (about 460 kJ/mol), and they do not break on boiling either way.
Covalent bonds do not break on boiling at all; if they did, the vapor would be a different substance.
A hydrogen bond is an attraction between molecules, far weaker than a covalent bond, not a kind of covalent bond.

why.correct: Two O–H groups give each molecule twice the sites for hydrogen bonding, so the molecules hold each other more strongly. (Its actual boiling point is 197 °C.)
options: Right: more hydrogen bonding per molecule, stronger attraction, higher boiling point.
Extra oxygen atoms add electrons, so they do not make the molecule less polarizable.
Similar mass is the "molar mass alone" trap; the number of hydrogen-bonding groups matters more here.
The O–H groups do not cancel; the molecule is polar, and each O–H can still hydrogen-bond.

why.correct: Halogen molecules are nonpolar, so their only attraction is London dispersion. From 18 to 106 electrons, the clouds get larger and easier to distort, so the momentary dipoles and the attractions get stronger.
options: Right: polarizability, from more electrons in more shells, sets the dispersion strength.
X–X molecules of one element have no polar bonds, so there are no permanent dipoles at all.
The bonds inside these molecules do not break on boiling, and their strengths do not follow the boiling points: F–F (159 kJ/mol) is weaker than Cl–Cl (243 kJ/mol), yet F₂ boils lower.
Gravity on a single molecule is negligible; the mass-only argument skips the real cause, polarizability.

why.correct: A substance is a liquid when room temperature lies between its melting and boiling points. Br₂ boils at 59 °C and melts at −7 °C, so it is liquid at 22 °C. I₂ boils at 184 °C but melts at 114 °C, so it is a solid.
options: Right: 22 °C is below its boiling point (59 °C) and above its melting point.
Cl₂ boils at −34 °C, so at 22 °C it is already a gas.
I₂ melts at 114 °C, so at 22 °C it is still a solid, even though its boiling point is high.
F₂ boils at −188 °C, so it is a gas at room temperature.

why.correct: F₂ (38.00 g/mol) and Ar (39.95 g/mol) both have 18 electrons and only dispersion forces. Equal electron counts give similar polarizability and similar boiling points (−188 °C and −186 °C).
options: Right: same electron count, similar polarizability, similar boiling point.
The pair shows the forces are similar, not that one kind of particle attracts more weakly.
Their molar masses differ (38.00 and 39.95 g/mol); the shared quantity is the electron count.
Argon has no H atoms and no polarity, so it cannot hydrogen-bond; dispersion is its only attraction.

why.correct: Boiling point rises with electron count down the noble gases: Ne (10) −246 °C, Ar (18) −186 °C, Kr (36) −153 °C. Xe (54) should be higher than Kr but still far below Br₂, a molecule with 70 electrons. The measured value is −108 °C.
options: Right: above krypton, as the trend requires.
This is below krypton's −153 °C, but xenon has more electrons and must boil higher.
This is near neon's value; it ignores the rise in dispersion forces with electron count.
This is bromine's boiling point; Br₂ has 70 electrons, more than xenon, so xenon should be well below it.

why.correct: A hydrogen bond runs from an H that is bonded to O on one molecule to the O (with its lone pairs) of a different molecule. W and X do this; Y joins two O atoms and Z joins two H atoms.
options: Right: an H on one molecule to the O of another.
Right: an H on one molecule to the O of another.
This joins two O atoms, both δ−, which repel; there is no H between them.
This joins two H atoms, both δ+, which repel; a hydrogen bond needs a lone pair on N, O or F as the partner.

why.correct: A hydrogen bond needs an H with a large δ+ (bonded to N, O or F) on one side and a lone pair on N, O or F on the other. Y joins two δ− O atoms, so it is a repulsion, not a hydrogen bond.
options: Right: like partial charges repel, and the bridging H is missing.
Length in a sketch is not the test; the atoms at the two ends are.
Hydrogen bonds are always between different molecules (or distant parts of a large one); an attraction inside a small molecule is a covalent bond, not a hydrogen bond.
Oxygen is one of the three atoms, N, O and F, that take part in hydrogen bonds.

why.correct: Boiling separates whole water molecules from their neighbors by overcoming the hydrogen bonds (and dispersion forces) between them. Steam is still H₂O.
options: Right: attractions between molecules are overcome; covalent bonds are not.
This is the "covalent bonds break on boiling" error; steam is made of H₂O molecules, not separate atoms.
The O–H bonds are about twenty times stronger than the attractions between molecules and stay intact at 100 °C.
Molecules in the vapor are far apart, so the attractions that held them in the liquid have been overcome.

why.correct: A hydrogen bond runs from the δ+ H of one molecule to a lone pair on the O of another. Rotating the molecule so its O faces that H turns the H…H repulsion into an H…O attraction.
options: Right: the H of one molecule must face the O of the other.
Pointing its H atoms away leaves no O facing the H on line Z.
Moving the molecule away weakens the repulsion but creates no attraction between H and O.
An attraction inside one molecule would be a covalent bond, and H₂O₂ is a different substance.

why.correct: Read the group 14 series: CH₄ −161.5 °C, SiH₄ −111.9 °C, GeH₄ −88.5 °C, SnH₄ −51.8 °C, a steady rise.
options: Right: each heavier hydride boils higher.
This reverses the direction of the trend shown on the graph.
That pattern belongs to the group 15 and 16 series, whose period 2 members are unusual.
The values span more than 100 °C, so the series is far from flat.

why.correct: Hydrogen bonds need H bonded to N, O or F. NH₃ and H₂O have them, so their boiling points jump above the trend; CH₄ is nonpolar and follows the dispersion trend.
options: Right: the high points come from hydrogen bonding, which methane cannot do.
CH₄ is the lightest in its group, which is why it boils lowest.
C–H bonds are nearly nonpolar, and methane is a symmetric, nonpolar molecule.
Carbon has fewer electrons (6) than nitrogen (7) or oxygen (8).

why.correct: From H₂S (18 electrons) to H₂Te (54 electrons) the molecules become much more polarizable, so dispersion forces increase. Their dipoles actually get smaller, because S, Se and Te are less electronegative than O, so the dispersion increase dominates.
options: Right: rising dispersion forces dominate in this series.
Hydrogen bonds need H bonded to N, O or F; S, Se and Te do not qualify.
Electronegativity falls down the group, so the molecules become less polar, not more.
Bonds inside the molecules do not break on boiling, and these bonds get weaker down the group.

why.correct: Electron count still sets dispersion strength. Water wins overall because each molecule also forms strong hydrogen bonds, which H₂Te cannot. The comparison must name every force in both substances.
options: Right: the extra force, hydrogen bonding, explains water's high boiling point.
Smaller molecules with fewer electrons are less polarizable, so their dispersion forces are weaker.
Boiling does not break the H–Te bonds; the molecules leave the liquid whole.
H₂O (18.02 g/mol) is much lighter than H₂Te (129.6 g/mol), so mass cannot explain it.

why.correct: Both have the formula C₅H₁₂, so the same electrons and mass. A long chain can lie alongside its neighbors over more of its length, so the momentary dipoles interact over a larger area.
options: Right: same electrons, more contact, stronger dispersion forces.
Isomers have the same formula and so the same number of electrons.
Both contain only C and H, with almost no polarity; neither has a meaningful dipole.
Isomers have identical molar masses.

why.correct: Every particle has electrons that can form momentary dipoles, so dispersion forces act between all particles. The others need polar molecules, N–H, O–H or F–H groups, or ions.
options: Right: momentary dipoles form in every electron cloud.
These need permanent dipoles, so they act between polar molecules.
These need H bonded to N, O or F on one molecule and a lone pair on N, O or F on another.
These need an ion and a polar molecule together.

why.correct: Methanol and ammonia have H bonded directly to N, O or F, plus a lone pair on that atom. In dimethyl ether and fluoromethane, every H is bonded to carbon. Cl is not one of the hydrogen-bonding atoms.
options: Right: its O–H hydrogen can bond to an O lone pair on a neighbor.
It has an O with lone pairs, but every H is on carbon, so no H carries a large enough δ+.
It has F, but the H atoms are on carbon, not on F, so it shows dipole-dipole forces instead.
H–Cl is polar, but Cl is not N, O or F; its attractions are dipole-dipole and dispersion.
Right: each N–H hydrogen can bond to the lone pair on the N of a neighbor.

why.correct: Both have 70 electrons, so their dispersion forces are similar. ICl is polar (I and Cl differ in electronegativity), so it adds dipole-dipole forces. It boils at 97 °C; Br₂ boils at 59 °C.
options: Right: the extra dipole-dipole forces decide it.
An even electron cloud means no permanent dipole, which is a reason for weaker, not stronger, attraction.
The masses differ by under 2%; the mass-only argument hides the real cause, polarity.
Equal electron counts make dispersion similar, but ICl also has dipole-dipole forces, so they differ.

why.correct: Methane (−162 °C) has 10 electrons and dispersion only; propane (−42 °C) has 26 electrons and dispersion only; dimethyl ether (−24 °C) is polar, adding dipole-dipole forces; ethanol (78 °C) adds hydrogen bonds through its O–H group.
A hydrogen bond is an attraction between molecules, not a covalent bond. It needs both an H on N, O or F and a lone pair on N, O or F.
options: Right: both conditions are named.
That describes an ordinary covalent bond such as C–H or O–H.
Two δ+ H atoms repel; the partner must be an N, O or F lone pair.
The H must itself be bonded to N, O or F; an H on carbon does not hydrogen-bond.

why.correct: Hydrogen bonds are strong per contact, but a large molecule with many electrons has strong total dispersion forces. Size can outweigh the kind of force.
options: Right: large dispersion forces can exceed hydrogen bonding in a small molecule.
Its H atoms are bonded to C, not N, O or F, so octane cannot hydrogen-bond.
C–H bonds are nearly nonpolar, and the molecule's shape cancels what little polarity there is.
No covalent bonds break on boiling.

why.correct: X melts low (114 °C), is soft and conducts in neither state. Low melting means only weak intermolecular forces hold the particles together, and no conduction means no ions or free electrons.
options: W conducts only when melted, the signature of an ionic solid whose ions become free to move.
Right: low melting point, soft, no conduction.
Y melts at 1,710 °C, far too high for a solid held by intermolecular forces.
Z conducts as a solid and bends, which marks a metal.

why.correct: In an ionic solid the charged particles are held in the lattice, so it cannot conduct until melting or dissolving frees the ions. A metal conducts as a solid because its electrons move freely.
options: Right: conduction only when melted is the ionic signature.
Many metals melt far above 801 °C (iron at 1,538 °C), so melting point does not separate the two.
Color is a weak test, and a powdered metal can look gray or dull.
Most metals are hard; hardness does not tell the two kinds apart. The test is brittleness and conduction.

why.correct: Only breaking covalent bonds explains a melting point near 1,710 °C in a nonconductor. In a covalent network, all valence electrons are in bonds, so nothing carries a charge.
options: Right: a covalent network solid such as quartz.
Hydrogen bonds are intermolecular forces; no molecular solid stays solid anywhere near 1,700 °C.
An ionic solid conducts once melted, and Y does not, so Y is not ionic.
A metal conducts as a solid because of its delocalized electrons; Y does not.

why.correct: In a metal the bonding is a sea of electrons shared by all the cations, so shifting a layer does not break it: the metal is malleable.
options: Right: the electron sea moves with the cations, so the solid bends instead of breaking.
Metals are not held by localized covalent bonds, so nothing has to break and re-form.
That repulsion is why ionic solids shatter; Z bends, so it is not ionic.
A molecular solid would crumble, not flatten; Z also conducts, which molecules cannot.

why.correct: A low melting point means only intermolecular forces hold the particles, so V is molecular, and no conduction when melted means it has no ions or free electrons. (Sucrose fits.)
options: Right: a low melting point points to intermolecular forces between molecules.
Melting a molecular solid overcomes intermolecular forces; its covalent bonds stay intact.
Right: a melted ionic or metallic solid would conduct.
A melted ionic solid conducts, and V does not.

why.correct: Box 4 shows metal cations among delocalized electrons. Those electrons move freely, so the solid conducts.
options: Neutral molecules carry no charge and there are no free electrons.
The ions in an ionic lattice are fixed, so box 2 conducts only when melted or dissolved.
In a covalent network every electron is in a bond, so nothing carries a charge.
Right: mobile electrons carry the current.

why.correct: Iodine is made of separate I₂ molecules. Each pair is joined by a covalent bond, and the pairs are held to each other only by dispersion forces.
options: Right: separate two-atom molecules.
Iodine contains no ions; I₂ is a neutral molecule of one element.
In a network every atom bonds to several neighbors; each iodine atom bonds to just one other.
Iodine is a nonmetal, so it has no cations in a sea of electrons.

why.correct: Melting a molecular solid pulls whole molecules apart; the bonds within each pair are untouched. Melting a network requires breaking covalent bonds, which takes far more energy.
options: Right: intermolecular forces versus covalent bonds.
Melting box 1 does not break its covalent bonds at all.
The number of atoms drawn is a sampling choice, not a cause of melting point.
Box 3 contains neutral atoms joined by covalent bonds; there are no ions.

why.correct: In an ionic lattice each ion is surrounded by opposite charges. Sliding one layer by one ion lines up + with + and − with −, and the repulsions break the crystal: ionic solids are brittle.
options: Right: repulsion between like charges after a shift.
Box 2 has no delocalized electrons; that describes a metal, which bends instead.
Box 2 contains ions, not molecules, and ionic bonds are strong.
Ionic solids are held by ionic, not covalent, bonds.

why.correct: The formulas look alike, but CO₂ forms small molecules and SiO₂ forms an endless network. Changing CO₂ to a gas pulls molecules apart; melting quartz breaks Si–O covalent bonds.
options: Right: molecular solid versus covalent network.
C=O bonds are polar too; and quartz has no separate molecules to attract.
Quartz has no separate molecules at all, so molecule mass is the wrong idea.
Si–O bonds are polar covalent, and molten quartz does not conduct like an ionic liquid.

why.correct: The atoms inside each molecule are covalently bonded, but separate molecules are held together by intermolecular forces.
options: Right: attractions between separate molecules.
That describes a covalent network solid.
That describes an ionic solid.
That describes a metallic solid.

why.correct: Diamond uses all four valence electrons of each C in localized bonds. Graphite uses three; the remaining electrons spread over the whole sheet and can move along it.
options: Right: delocalized electrons within each graphite layer.
Both contain neutral carbon atoms; there are no carbon ions.
Diamond is a covalent network held entirely by covalent bonds.
Graphite is a covalent network with delocalized electrons, not a metal.

why.correct: A crystal's ordered pattern gives every particle the same environment, so it melts sharply. In an amorphous solid like glass the environments vary, so it softens over a range.
options: Right: gradual softening marks an amorphous solid such as glass.
Molecules all melting at once would give a sharp melting point, not a range.
Conductivity says nothing about whether melting is sharp or gradual.
A pure crystalline solid has a sharp melting point; it does not lack one.

why.correct: Methane (−182 °C) is molecular with dispersion forces only; ice (0 °C) is molecular with hydrogen bonds; NaCl (801 °C) is ionic; diamond (above 3,500 °C) is a covalent network.
Sucrose and CO₂ are made of separate molecules. SiC is a covalent network, KBr is ionic and copper is metallic.
options: Right: separate sucrose molecules.
SiC is a hard covalent network like diamond.
KBr is a metal with a nonmetal: an ionic solid.
Right: separate CO₂ molecules (dry ice).
Copper is a metal: cations in a sea of electrons.

why.correct: Naphthalene is nonpolar (dispersion only, 68 electrons). Urea has only 32 electrons, but its N–H hydrogens bond to the O and N lone pairs of neighbors. Hydrogen bonding outweighs the smaller dispersion forces.
options: Right: hydrogen bonds explain it, not mass.
The question states urea is molecular; 133 °C is far too low for a network.
Urea has 32 electrons and naphthalene 68, so dispersion favors naphthalene.
Urea is made of neutral molecules; containing N does not make a compound ionic.

why.correct: Ice is a molecular solid. Liquid water is still made of H₂O molecules, so no O–H bond broke; hydrogen bonds between molecules were partly overcome.
options: Right: melting a molecular solid overcomes attractions between molecules.
Water molecules are covalent, not ionic; melting does not form ions.
Ice is molecular: separate H₂O molecules held by hydrogen bonds.
Melting loosens all the attractions between molecules, including many hydrogen bonds.

why.correct: At every temperature water has the lowest vapor pressure, so the fewest molecules escape: its molecules attract each other most strongly.
options: Ether has the highest vapor pressure, so its attractions are the weakest of the three.
Ethanol's vapor pressure is higher than water's at every temperature shown, so its attractions are weaker.
Right: lowest vapor pressure at every temperature.
The three curves are far apart, so the attractions clearly differ.

why.correct: The normal boiling point is where the vapor pressure reaches 760 torr (1 atm). The ether curve reaches 760 torr at 34.6 °C.
A liquid boils when its vapor pressure equals the pressure above it. Water's vapor pressure reaches 355 torr at 80 °C.
options: At 60 °C water's vapor pressure is 149 torr, still below 355 torr.
Right: the vapor pressure equals the 355 torr air pressure at 80 °C.
100 °C is the boiling point at 760 torr, sea-level pressure.
Lower air pressure lowers the boiling point; it does not raise it.

why.correct: Both liquids hydrogen-bond, but water forms more hydrogen bonds per molecule (two H on O and two lone pairs) than ethanol (one H on O). Weaker overall attractions let more ethanol molecules escape, so its vapor pressure is higher.
options: Right: weaker attractions, more escape, higher vapor pressure.
Heavier molecules at the same temperature move more slowly, not faster; and mass is not the cause here.
Ethanol has an O–H group, so it does hydrogen-bond; it just forms fewer per molecule than water.
Evaporation leaves molecules whole; no covalent bonds break.

why.correct: Each curve bends upward: water rises 37.8 torr from 20 °C to 40 °C but 206 torr from 60 °C to 80 °C. Above the normal boiling point the vapor pressure keeps rising (that is why a pressure cooker works).
options: Right: rising and curving upward.
Water rises 37.8 torr from 20 to 40 °C but 206 torr from 60 to 80 °C, so the rise is not even.
Every curve is above zero at 0 °C; liquids have a vapor pressure at every temperature.
Vapor pressure keeps rising above 760 torr in a sealed container; 760 torr is just where an open liquid boils.

why.correct: In a liquid the molecules touch but are jumbled, and they settle into the bottom of the container: box R.
options: P shows molecules far apart throughout the box: a gas.
Q shows molecules touching in a regular pattern: a solid.
Right: touching and disordered, taking the container's shape.
Q is ordered like a solid, so only R fits a liquid.

why.correct: Q is a solid and P is a gas. Solid directly to gas is sublimation.
options: Right: solid to gas.
Melting turns a solid (Q) into a liquid (R), not a gas.
Condensation turns a gas into a liquid.
Deposition is the reverse change, gas to solid.

why.correct: Squeezing a gas removes empty space between molecules. In a solid or liquid the molecules already touch, so there is almost no empty space to remove.
options: Right: gases are mostly empty space.
They are the same molecules in all three boxes, and the same size.
Molecules in solids and liquids are held by intermolecular forces, not covalent bonds to each other.
How fast the molecules move is not what makes a gas compressible, and slow-moving gas molecules are not easier to push together. The empty space between gas molecules is what can be squeezed out.

why.correct: Vaporization separates molecules from each other by overcoming intermolecular forces. The molecules themselves are unchanged in size and composition.
options: Right: the molecules separate but are not changed.
Covalent bonds do not break in vaporization; the gas is the same substance.
The molecules stay the same size; the space between them grows.
Vaporization needs energy to overcome attractions; it does not form them.

why.correct: 742 torr × (1 atm / 760 torr) = 0.97632 atm, which is 0.976 atm to three significant figures.
2.35 atm × (101.325 kPa / 1 atm) = 238.11 kPa, which is 238 kPa to three significant figures.
Only temperature (and the identity of the liquid) changes a vapor pressure. The amount of liquid and the container size do not, as long as some liquid remains.

variables.name: Raise the temperature to 40 °C
variables.why: More molecules move fast enough to escape, so more are in the gas at equilibrium: 23.8 torr at 25 °C rises to 55.3 torr at 40 °C.

variables.name: Add more liquid water at 25 °C
variables.why: Vapor pressure depends on the liquid and the temperature, not on the amount of liquid. Escape and return balance at the same gas pressure.

variables.name: Move all of it, still at 25 °C, into a larger sealed flask with liquid left over
variables.why: More water evaporates to fill the larger space, but at equilibrium the pressure of the vapor returns to the same value at the same temperature.

why.correct: Molecules in a liquid have a range of speeds. At any temperature, some at the surface can escape, so every liquid has a vapor pressure. Boiling only requires that this vapor pressure reach the outside pressure.
options: Right: liquids have a vapor pressure at every temperature.
A liquid's vapor pressure depends only on its present temperature, not its history.
Puddles dry at room temperature because water molecules themselves escape.
760 torr is the vapor pressure only at the normal boiling point, 100 °C.

why.correct: Pentane has 42 electrons and hexane 50. Pentane's weaker dispersion forces let more molecules escape, so its vapor pressure is higher (about 512 torr against 151 torr).
options: Right: weaker attractions, higher vapor pressure.
Heavier molecules at the same temperature move more slowly, and hexane's stronger dispersion forces hold it back.
Pentane has no H on N, O or F, so it cannot hydrogen-bond; and attractions hold molecules in, not push them out.
Nonpolar molecules still attract by dispersion forces, and those differ.

why.correct: A liquid boils when its vapor pressure matches the pressure above it; the normal boiling point uses 1 atm.
options: Right: vapor pressure matches 1 atm of outside pressure.
Liquids evaporate at every temperature, far below the boiling point.
A liquid's vapor pressure is above zero at every temperature.
Under higher pressure, as in a pressure cooker, a liquid stays liquid above its normal boiling point.

why.correct: Melting, sublimation and evaporation overcome attractions between particles, so they need energy. Condensation, freezing and deposition form attractions and release energy.
options: Right: attractions in the solid are overcome.
Gas particles are captured by attractions, which releases energy.
Right: solid to gas overcomes attractions.
Particles settle into fixed positions, releasing energy.
Right: molecules must overcome their neighbors' attractions to escape.
Gas to solid releases energy as attractions form.

why.correct: Vapor pressure follows the strength of attractions, not mass. Water's hydrogen bonds hold its molecules more tightly than Br₂'s dispersion forces, so fewer water molecules escape.
options: Right: name the forces in both substances.
Mass does not set vapor pressure; the attractions do, and here they favor water.
At the same temperature heavier molecules move more slowly, not faster.
Evaporation leaves Br₂ molecules whole; bromine vapor is Br₂.

why.correct: Vapor pressure depends only on the liquid and its temperature. More molecules escape at a higher temperature; the amount of liquid, the flask size and other gases do not change the equilibrium pressure of the water vapor.
options: Right: faster molecules escape more often.
The vapor pressure does not depend on the amount of liquid.
More water evaporates, but the vapor pressure returns to the same value.
Nitrogen adds to the pressure in the flask, but the water's vapor pressure is unchanged.

why.correct: T = 98.6 + 273.15 = 371.75 K; P = 742.0 torr × (1 atm / 760 torr) = 0.97632 atm; V = 0.2480 L. n = PV/RT = (0.97632 atm × 0.2480 L) / (0.08206 L·atm/(mol·K) × 371.75 K) = 0.0079371 mol, which is 0.007937 mol. (98.6 °C is known to the tenths place, so the sum is 371.8 K, four significant figures; report four.)
M = mass / moles = 0.4625 g / 0.007937 mol = 58.271 g/mol, which is 58.27 g/mol to four significant figures.
Moles come from P, V and T, which are unaffected. The mass found by difference includes the extra liquid, so it is too large, and mass ÷ moles is too large.
options: Right: the error is in the mass only, and it is too large.
The moles of vapor depend only on P, V and T of the flask, which did not change.
Mass is part of the calculation, and it is wrong here.
The moles are calculated from PV/RT; the extra liquid changes only the mass.

why.correct: The calculated molar mass, 58.27 g/mol, lies close to acetone's 58.08 g/mol and far from the other two.
options: Right: the data point to acetone.
All three boil below 98.6 °C, so boiling point cannot pick one; the molar mass can.
The mass of vapor alone says nothing until it is divided by the moles, which gives acetone's value.
Experimental values carry small errors; a value within about 1% identifies the liquid.

why.correct: Heating adds no moles, so every mole fraction stays at its value. At constant V, each partial pressure is proportional to kelvin temperature, so P(O₂) rises by 360.15/300.15 = 1.20 times.
options: Right: same moles, higher pressure.
Mole fractions depend only on the amounts of gas, which did not change.
The mole fraction cannot change without changing the amounts; the pressure does change.
Pressure depends on temperature at constant volume, so it rises.

why.correct: Each gas acts as if alone: P(N₂) = n(N₂)RT/V, and none of those changed. The total pressure rises and X(N₂) falls, and the two effects cancel exactly.
options: Right: P(N₂) depends only on its own moles, V and T.
X(N₂) does fall, but the total pressure rises in proportion, so their product is unchanged.
The total rises because of the helium, not because N₂ pushes harder.
Ideal gas particles take up negligible volume, so helium does not crowd out the nitrogen.

why.correct: Doubling T from 200 K to 400 K doubles P from 0.821 to 1.641 atm, and the line points back to zero pressure at 0 K: P = (nR/V) × T.
options: Right: P/T is constant, as PV = nRT predicts at fixed n and V.
Inverse proportion would make P fall as T rises.
The ratio P/T is the same at every point, so the rise is steady, not slowing.
In °C the line would not pass through zero; only kelvin gives proportionality.

why.correct: (0.100 mol × 0.08206 L·atm/(mol·K) × 500. K) / 2.00 L = 2.0515 atm, which is 2.05 atm. Or extend the line: P/T = 0.0041 atm/K.
Shifting every temperature by 273.15 slides the line sideways without bending it, so it still reaches zero pressure at 0 K, which is −273.15 °C.
options: Right: same straight line, shifted.
At 0 °C (273 K) the gas still has a large pressure, so the line cannot pass through the origin.
A Celsius degree is the same size as a kelvin, so the slope does not change and no bend appears.
Pressure depends on temperature in any scale; only the zero point differs.

why.correct: At fixed V, P = (nR/V)T. Doubling n doubles the slope nR/V, so every pressure doubles.
options: Right: P is proportional to n at fixed V and T.
More gas particles hit the walls more often, so pressure rises, not falls.
